item.title: When I die
item.description:
When I die, I do not want to be cremated; I want to be buried. And not too deep; so that from my rotting body, flowers shall grow; and I will be in them; and that, is eternity.

I think many years ago I stumbled upon this saying on the interwebz.

A search for these words nowadays does not yield that saying anymore, so I am posting it anew.

The part after "so that" was famously said by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch. (paraphrase; cf. MM T 365, page 1 and MM T 2547, page 60, eMunch.no.)

His name is pronounced in English as "Moonk". He is the same artist who gave us the painting The Scream.

Cremation offers many options; for example, the ashes of Maria Calas, were scattered over the Aegean sea in 1979, according to her wishes. That is a wonderful way to go.

Burial, however, is regulated. It can only be done in specific places, at a specific depth, (usually about 1.2 m,) and graves are cleared every 10 or 20 years to make room for new ones. I think that this is a certain form of pandemic misery.

I am glad to see that in The Netherlands there is an option to have a natural burial site (natuurbegraafplaats) which also seems to involve the notion of a permanent resting spot. I will inquire prices when the time seems to approach.

item.title: Claude Code
item.description:
A few words of amazement about Claude Code...

In a pet project at home, I had a little app that rendered something on the screen, and one day I decided to rewrite it to use a different rendering technology. The rewrite went well, but it was very difficult, so by the time I was done, I was tired and fed up with it. One little visual thing was missing from the new app, but I did not want to bother with it. I just put the whole project on ice.

That was before the A.I. boom.

Now in the era of A.I., I decided to revisit that project, and to ask Claude Code to add that little visual thingy for me.

As the case usually is with A.I. prompts, if you make them detailed and technical you are likely to get what you want, whereas if you make them high-level you might save time in formulating the prompt, but you might not be satisfied with the results you will get. I tried to test this by going very high-level.

I gave Claude Code a screenshot of the old app and a screenshot of the new app, I used a couple of words to identify the little visual thingy that was present in the old app, and I asked her1 how she would go about adding it to the new app. Amazingly, she understood the screenshots and offered an approach for achieving what I asked.

I found the proposed approach very reasonable, so I typed:

Excellent! As Captain Piccard would say, make it so!

She responded:

Engaging...

After working on it for a few seconds, to my astonishment, Claude Code launched the new app and took a screenshot to see the results of her work. The results were off by a few pixels, so Claude Code reported this, and asked me for the go-ahead to fix it. I agreed, so she worked on it for a few more seconds, and then she launched the new app again, and took another screenshot to confirm that she had done it right.

I also checked every single line of code that she wrote, and everything was perfect.

That entire interaction was nothing short of mind-blowing.

Then, Claude Code asked me how she did in that session, and I chose "good", and then she asked me to type some feedback. This is what I wrote:

I am very amazed. I had been promised flying cars. They were not given to me. But this is even better.

  1. Referring to Claude by "her": Claude is genderless, but as a hetero male I have very predictably configured a female voice for it, therefore Claude is a "she" for me. ↩︎

item.title: Notes on "How to be charismatic" by Charles Duhigg
item.description:
Ignore the clickbait title and cover image: this is simply a little technique for being more likable.

Might be useful to those of us who have a deficit in this area, people in the autistic spectrum who are mistaken for narcissists, etc.

The video is only 9 minutes long.

Here it is: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y7dNhT1XMqw

My notes

  • Presence
    • Not Surface Questions, but Deep Questions instead.
      • Surface Questions are about facts of life.
      • Deep Questions are about values, beliefs, experiences.
      • Not "where do you work?" but instead "what is the best part of your job?"
      • Not "what hospital are you working at?" but instead "what made you decide to become a doctor?"
  • Warmth
    • "Looping for understanding"
      • Ask a question, (preferably a deep question,) and listen to the answer.
      • Repeat the answer in your own words.
      • Ask if you got it right.
  • Vulnerability

    • Offer one small, true thing you'd normally keep back.

      • A doubt
      • A mistake you made
      • Something you are nervous about

      ...and let a self-deprecating joke carry it.

My thoughts

Of course, all this is easier said than done:

  • When looking for a deep question to ask, you are likely to draw a blank.

    • So, the person is in sales. What deep question can you possibly ask to someone in sales?
    • So, the person is a chemist, specializing in petrochemistry. What the f***k do you know about petrochemistry?

  • If you ask a question, receive an answer, and try repeating the answer in your own words, chances are that the other person will tell you that you missed some point, and will re-answer to set the record straight. So, now you start repeating their new answer, but while you are at it, they again find something to add, etc. So, you might never get to ask if you got it right. Following simple steps looks nice as an exercise on paper, but it rarely works as intended in reality.

  • When trying to offer a small, true thing you'd normally keep back, you run the danger of undershooting or overshooting.

    • Undershooting means ending up saying something which is actually self-praise instead of self-deprecation, coming across as an insufferable narcissist.
    • Overshooting means ending up saying something which is way too embarrassing, and coming across as a complete jerk.

  • At the end of all this, we are left with one suggestion: to practice the technique. But how can you practice something like that?

    • I suppose there is only one way, which is to start communicating with random people and trying out the technique; however, there is an element of dishonesty here:
      • Communicating with people not because you have a genuine interest in them, but merely because you want to try out a communication technique.
      • Using people as guinea pigs for your own conversational experiments.
      • Running the risk of giving people a lousy conversational experience (of course, since you are practicing) and being indifferent to it.

item.title: You Want It Darker
item.description:
Leonard Cohen died in November of 2016, a mere few weeks after the release of his last record, You Want it Darker. The homonymous song of that record greatly surprised me, and revealed to me a Leonard Cohen that I was previously unaware of.

When I like the art produced by an artist, I tend to confine my interest to the art, rather than the artist. I guess I learned this lesson as a teenager, in the early nineteen-eighties, from the first book I ever bought, using my own pocket money: No One Here Gets Out Alive, the life and death of Jim Morrison. Contrary to my expectations, once I was done reading the book I decided that there was really nothing to take home from it. This, then, became a broader theme throughout my life: I have always been very weary of cults of personality and I will almost never state that I am a fan of anyone.

I say almost never, because proclaiming that nobody is worthy of admiration shows lack of appreciation for some undeniably great humans, and depending on how you mean it, it constitutes either hubris or nihilism.

So, I may, on a rare occasion, call myself a fan of someone. However, I only do so posthumously, because it is only after someone's death that we can be sure that they will not do anything stupid to disappoint us.

This is, for example, why I can say with confidence that I am a fan of Bertrand Russel, while I never said that I am a fan of Elon Musk, no matter how much I liked the guy. (And recent developments vindicate my choice amply, to say the least.)

Also, Richard Dawkins has certainly earned his laurels, but technically he is on my waiting list for as long as he is still breathing. (And in case you are wondering, no, his recent brushes with the wokes, regarding exactly how many sexes exist, which nearly resulted in him being cancelled, did not change my opinion about him at all; if anything, I have even more respect for him now.)

So, the way it went with Leonard Cohen is that I have always liked his music, but I have known very little about the man.

  • I have known him as Canadian, but that is the most basic thing you can know about someone.

  • I have known that he owns a home on the island of Hydra, where he spent a part of his life, but that is something that you cannot fail to know about him if you are Greek.

  • I have known that he is Jewish, but I have not known whether he identified as such by religion, or by heritage, or just by upbringing environment. Furthermore, I have not sought to clarify this, because I would rather leave his personal life alone.

  • I have known him as a leftist, but there are many examples of leftists who were to some degree religious.

  • I have known him as being anti-establishment, but I had no idea whether he considered god as part of the establishment.

  • I have known that he makes some religious references in his songs, but I did not have any grounds to doubt the sincerity of the references.

So, from all that I knew about him, I had no reason to suspect that he had any beef whatsoever with religion, or with god in particular.

When I discovered the song You Want it Darker on YouTube I started playing it in the background, intending to do other things while listening to it, but as soon as I realized what the lyrics were saying I jumped in my seat. I listened to it again. And again. I found the lyrics and read them. To my astonishment, I realized that the song was a fierce condemnation and rejection of the Judeo-Christian god.

The criticism in the song is not directed only towards organized religion, or only towards its followers; it is also largely directed to god himself: it is personal. And it is not just a denial: it is anathema. The song competes with old favorites of mine like Dear God by XTC, Orgasmatron by Motörhead, and God Was Never On Your Side, also by Motörhead. I cannot imagine a more poetic way of telling god to, uhm, basically, fuck off.

Acknowledging the fact that Leonard Cohen's lyrics were often enigmatic, and the fact that we tend to interpret enigmatic lyrics according to our own belief systems, I searched around for more information about the song, trying to find out what others are saying about it. Sure enough, various folks interpret the song in whatever way suits their prejudices. I found a religious web site where someone explains the song as an affirmation of Leonard Cohen's faith; so, that person listened to the same song that I listened to, and yet took home from it the exact opposite of what I took home. Great, just great.

Clearly, there must be ways of interpreting the song that are right, and ways that are wrong; but how can we tell?

Well, according to Wikipedia, Alexis Petridis, the head critic for rock and pop music at The Guardian described the song as "a menacing critique of religion".

But what do critics know, right?

And besides, everyone knows that Wikipedia is unreliable, right?

So, let us look at the lyrics, shall we?

Artist: Leonard Cohen
Song: You Want It Darker (2016)

If you are the dealer, I'm out of the game
If you are the healer, it means I'm broken and lame
If thine is the glory, then mine must be the shame
You want it darker
We kill the flame

Magnified, sanctified
Be thy holy name
Vilified, crucified
In the human frame
A million candles burning
For the help that never came
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

There's a lover in the story
But the story's still the same
There's a lullaby for suffering
And a paradox to blame
But it's written in the scriptures
And it's not some idle claim
You want it darker
We kill the flame

They're lining up the prisoners
And the guards are taking aim
I struggle with some demons
They were middle class and tame
I didn't know I had permission
To murder and to maim
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

Magnified, sanctified
Be thy holy name
Vilified, crucified
In the human frame
A million candles burning
For the love that never came
You want it darker
We kill the flame

If you are the dealer, let me out of the game
If you are the healer, I'm broken and lame
If thine is the glory, mine must be the shame
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

For those who read the lyrics above and are still unsure, here is an explanation of it all, verse by verse, courtesy of yours truly. Of course, my interpretation may be subject to my own prejudices, so please, by all means, leave a comment and tell me where you think I am wrong.

  • If you are the dealer, I'm out of the game
    If you are the healer, it means I'm broken and lame
    If thine is the glory, then mine must be the shame

    These verses constitute outright denial of god: whatever it is that god stands for, Leonard Cohen wants to have nothing to do with it. A reference is also being made to the biblical significance of repeating something three times as signaling a decree that is fully settled and impossible to ignore.

  • You want it darker
    We kill the flame

    These verses can be interpreted as saying that religion demands a worsening of the human condition, and its followers seem to be happy to abide to the absolute degree. The flame may allegorically refer to religion's historical opposition to enlightenment, the inescapable conclusion being that religiosity necessarily implies a dumbing down of the world. In this sense, the flame is the same as the one mentioned by another favorite Jew of mine in his own famous scathing critique of superstitious belief: The Demon-Haunted World (Science as a Candle in the Dark) by Carl Sagan. The light may also be a reference to the singer's own impending death, by way of that one poem by Dylan Thomas.

  • Magnified, sanctified
    Be thy holy name
    Vilified, crucified
    In the human frame

    "Magnified and sanctified be His great name" are the opening words of the Kaddish, a prayer central to Jewish liturgy and entirely absent from the Christian literature. The crucifixion, on the other hand, is an exclusively Christian thing, and entirely absent from the Jewish literature. Thus, these two verses establish a Judeo-Christian perspective, rather than a purely Jewish one or a purely Christian one. Obviously, Leonard Cohen has an axe to grind with both. This becomes important a bit further down.

  • A million candles burning
    For the help that never came

    This points out the folly of going through the motions of worshiping a god who is entirely absent. It also constitutes the first reference in this song of the great philosophical / theological Problem of Evil, otherwise known as the Epicurean Paradox: how is it possible to reconcile the existence of evil and suffering in this world with the notion of a supposedly omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent god? (Spoiler: it is not possible.)

  • Hineni, hineni
    I'm ready, my Lord

    Hineni is a Hebrew word which means "here I am". It is the response given by various important biblical figures, such as Abraham, upon being called by god in various chapters of the bible. In Leonard Cohen's own words, (from the official You Want It Darker press conference,) it is "a declaration of readiness, no matter what the outcome."

  • There's a lover in the story
    But the story's still the same

    The lover is obviously Jesus, since a previous verse established a Judeo-Christian context rather than a purely Jewish one. To say that the story is still the same is to say that the addition of Jesus in the New Testament does not erase the cruelty of the scriptures, nor the cruelty of the god manifested by those scriptures, and it has done nothing to lessen the historical cruelty of the followers.

  • There's a lullaby for suffering
    And a paradox to blame

    The lullaby for suffering may refer to the perverse fascination of the Christian religion with guilt to the point of self-torture. The paradox may refer either to the Epicurean Paradox, or to the famously nonsensical concept of the Original Sin.

  • But it's written in the scriptures
    And it's not some idle claim

    This is stating that all the perverse, wrongful, and inhuman things written in the scriptures cannot be simply brushed aside, and the religion has to be judged by what its own scriptures say. (If modern legal systems were to actually do that, then all Abrahamic religions would have to be outlawed as criminal organizations for incitement to hatred, racism, violence, mutilation, murder, and genocide, to name just a few of the offenses.)

  • They're lining up the prisoners
    And the guards are taking aim

    This is very obviously a reference to the holocaust.

  • I struggle with some demons
    They were middle class and tame

    The demons here are probably the conscience of all those who witnessed the holocaust and yet kept minding their own business, allowing it to happen.

  • I didn't know I had permission
    To murder and to maim

    This must be a reference to several notable accounts in the bible where god explicitly instructs the Israelites to commit genocide against their neighboring nations.

While researching the song I learned a few details about the circumstances under which it was made, which surprised me all the more. During the last year of Leonard Cohen's life, his deteriorating health severely restricted his mobility; so, the living room of his home was turned into a recording studio to allow him to sing while seated or reclining.

This means that the record was created while Leonard Cohen was fully aware that his end was near.

There is not a shadow of a doubt that when he says "I am ready, my Lord" he is acknowledging his own imminent death.

Now, usually, people on their deathbed do not tend to pick that as the best moment to break ties with god. Or should I say, to burn their bridges with god. Or perhaps, in his particular case, should I say, to napalm-bomb their bridges with god.

So, the making of this song by Leonard Cohen at the very end of his life seems to be the exact antithesis of a death-bed conversion.

Perhaps good old Leonard associated with religion during his life purely out of social interest, (like my own father did,) which may have given people some false impressions, so perhaps he wanted to set the record straight before departing.

He surely did.

In no uncertain terms.

I take my hat off to him.

The man: Leonard Cohen (Wikipedia)
The record: You Want it Darker (Wikipedia)
The song: Yow Want it Darker (Song) (Wikipedia)

item.title: The Bud Winter Sleeping Technique
item.description:
Sometimes I have trouble sleeping, and this can have severe consequences the following day, especially if it is a workday.

For a long time I had been thinking that techniques must have been devised for helping people fall asleep, especially in high-stakes settings such as professional sports, key value driving professions, the military, etc. This means that finding such a technique is probably just a matter of a brief internet research. However, this idea would always occur to me while lying in bed, trying to fall asleep, which is never the right time to get up and start doing internet research.

One day, while catching up with my friend Freek (a co-worker from a long time ago, when we used to work at TopDesk) I brought this up to him, and he searched for it right then and there, on his phone. He immediately found this technique, developed by famous U.S. track coach Bud Winter, originally intended to help Olympic athletes relax, and later adopted by the U.S. military. It can, supposedly, make someone fall asleep within a couple of minutes.

The technique is quite simple, but it requires consistent daily practice to train your nervous system to flip the "sleep switch". Reports have allegedly shown that in the military, after 6 weeks of exercising this method daily, it has a success rate of around 96%. If that is true, it is phenomenal.

So, I created an adaptation of Bud Winter's technique, for listening when going to sleep, the goal being to eventually be able to recall it from memory and to not have a need for the recording anymore.

In my adaptation, the text has been converted into a flat list of instructions, suitable for following along as you are listening to it. To do this, I had to remove some phrases that are unsuitable for do-as-you-listen narration.

I have also added a few more steps at the end about additional sensory detail, which I saw proposed somewhere, and seems like a very good idea.

One minor change I made to the original list of steps is that I moved the steps about relaxing the arms after the step about settling the torso, because I found that in order to settle my torso I often have to use my arms, but then I need to repeat the relaxing of the arms, so why not change the order so that the hands only need relaxing once.

So, here is my adaptation of the Bud Winter technique for falling asleep:

  • Close your eyes.
  • Breathe slowly.
  • Relax your forehead,
    • your jaw,
    • your tongue,
    • and the muscles around your eyes.
  • Let your shoulders drop as low as they can go,
    • as if they are sinking into the bed.
  • Relax your neck.
  • Settle your torso.
  • Take a deep breath,
    • and exhale.
  • Relax your stomach muscles,
    • and let go of any tension you are holding in your torso.
  • Let your upper and lower arms go limp on one side,
    • followed by the other.
  • Relax your hands,
    • and fingers.
  • Relax your right thigh,
    • then your right calf,
    • right ankle,
    • and right foot.
  • Relax your left thigh,
    • then your left calf,
    • left ankle,
    • and left foot.
  • Your entire body should now feel heavy and limp.
  • Imagine yourself lying flat on your back in a canoe,
    • on a calm, serene lake,
    • with nothing but a clear blue sky above you.
  • Bring to your mind the sounds of the setting:
    • gentle waves lapping at your boat,
    • birds calling and chirping,
    • frogs croaking from the shore,
    • an insect buzzing by,
    • indistinct, joyful human voices from a distant boat.
  • Bring to your mind the smells of the setting:
    • the cool humid air,
    • the wet wood from the boat,
    • soil, moss, and grass from the shoreline,
    • green notes from water plants and trees around the lake.

I have tried the technique a few times so far, and each time I am surprised to find that certain groups of muscles, for example the muscles around my eyes, have been in tension up until that moment, and they would have remained in tension for who knows how long, had the narration not brought them to my attention. So, it seems like it does really help.

I created an mp3 file so that I can listen to it when going to sleep.

Here is version 2, which constitutes a considerable improvement over version 1:

Here is how I made it:

For converting the text to speech, I used the MAI (Microsoft AI) playground because it is free, and it is incredibly, astonishingly, mind-blowingly good. I experimented a bit and found that voice "Harper" with style "Softvoice" produced excellent results for my purposes. It does have a limit on the amount of text that it will process, so I had to do two prompts and receive two audio files.

For editing the audio, I used Audacity because it is a well-known, free, decently capable, and acceptably bug-free audio editor. Here is what I did in terms of audio editing:

  1. I aggressively de-essed the speech by adding the Bass and Treble realtime effect, and setting the dial for treble to -20dB.
    • (In version 1 I had used the Filter Curve EQ effect to cut out everything above about 5 kilohertz, but later I decided that this was way too aggressive.)
  2. I slowed down the speech to 90% of what it was.
    • (In version 1 I used 80%, but later I decided that this was too slow.)
  3. I inserted one second of silence between most phrases, in order to give the listener plenty of time to follow each instruction before the next instruction starts.
  4. I mixed it with the music. (See below.)

For the music, I used Google Gemini, because it is one of the few services that a) actually work, and b) do actually understand what I mean when I say "in the style of Brian Eno's ambient music". It only creates 30-second tracks, which is a joke, but for my purposes it was okay because ambient music can be repeated over and over again, especially when it is in the background with human voice in the foreground.

I decided that music is necessary as an introduction, in order to give me some time from the moment I press "play" on the bedside phone, to turn off the light, lie on the bed, and cover myself with the quilt before the actual instructions start playing. (In the beginning I was thinking of using several seconds of silence before the instructions begin, but I quickly realized that this would not work, because the problem with silence is that you never know whether you have actually started it, or whether you made a mistake and nothing is happening.)

Finding an A.I. service that would generate the music according to my specifications, and for free, was the hardest part.

  • Most generative A.I. services out there simply do not generate music.
  • ChatGPT said that it could not do it, then it added that it was capable of doing it with some workarounds. However, when I asked it to try some of those workarounds I realized that it was only wasting my time. There is no way to get ChatGPT to generate music.
  • Suno and MusicGPT (no affiliation with ChatGPT) failed to understand my instructions, and created audio that was not what I wanted. (Yes, so maybe they refused to follow my instructions, due to copyright concerns, but refusal without a clear explanation is miserable failure in my book.)
  • Udio demanded that I enable DRM on my browser, (I should have refused right then and there,) and once I did that, it went ahead and created some music which was decently close to what I had asked for, but it would, of course, not let me have it. How debauched is that?
  • Soundraw does not seem to offer a text box to describe what you want in text; instead, it follows a multiple choice quiz approach, which is, of course, so stupendously limited as to be completely useless for my purposes.
  • Only Google Gemini worked for me, although for most purposes, its 30-second limitation makes it about as useless as the rest.

I will leave you with a quote from Bud Winter:

Demand perfection of yourself and you will seldom attain it.
Fear of making a mistake is the biggest single cause of making one.
Relax: pursue excellence, not perfection.

— Lloyd (Bud) Winter

item.title: The Heron and the Hawk
item.description:
Around the turn of the millennium me and my girlfriend at the time, Angelica, decided to spend an Easter vacation in Aegina, a beautiful and serene little island just south of Athens. During that period of time Angelica was volunteering for the Greek Center for the Protection of Wild Animals (Ελληνικό Κέντρο Περίθαλψης Αγρίων Ζώων / ΕΚΠΑΖ / EKPAZ) in Athens, and we had both been volunteers at Greenpeace Greece for several years already. As such, we were in a sense insiders of the relatively small environmental movement of Greece. So, we were told that while we were in Aegina we could go visit the new facilities of EKPAZ on the island; they would be closed to the public due to Easter, but the personnel would be there, and they would be happy to receive us and show us around.

In previous years, EKPAZ had been housed in a very old building in the town of Aegina. Built in 1828, only one year after the modern Greek state was formed, it was the first public building, and for a long time the largest building in the country. It was originally built as an orphanage, then used for various purposes such as military academy, psychiatric hospital, quarantine station, refugee asylum, etc. but starting from 1880, and for more than a hundred years, it was a jailhouse, primarily receiving political prisoners.
Aerial view of the old jailhouse of Aegina; photo from wikimedia commons
Street view of the old jailhouse of Aegina; photo from lalaounistravel.com
Inside view of the old jailhouse of Aegina during the EKPAZ years; photo from ethnos.gr

The jail was shut down in 1985 by the newly elected socialist government, and after that the building remained unused, because it required a very expensive restoration that nobody could afford. So, in 1990 the municipality allowed EKPAZ to use it as an asylum for injured wild animals, the idea being, I suppose, that the animals would not mind the decrepit state of the facilities.

Then the municipality started making plans to turn the old building into a museum, so in 2001 they had EKPAZ relocate. This time the municipality granted EKPAZ a recently constructed building complex located on a gentle hillside in a somewhat remote and inland location of Aegina. The complex was originally intended as a cultural center, but it had never materialized as such.
The new facilities of EKPAZ, early 2000s; photo from ekpaz.com
The new facilities of EKPAZ, (zoom,) early 2000s; photo from ekpaz.com

I cannot say that I know how and why this cultural center that apparently nobody had a need for had popped up in the middle of nowhere, but it seemed to me like one more of those projects that are unfortunately common in Greece, which are undertaken with the sole intention of misappropriating European Union funds. The standard play is that a proposal is submitted for a work for which the EU will provide a 50% subsidy; the work is completed for only 10% of the cost, another 20% or so goes to pay taxes, (because invoices are issued for 100% of the cost, to justify the 50% funding,) and the remaining 20% or so, which may amount to hundreds of thousands of Euros, goes into the pockets of those involved in the fraud. The end-result is invariably useless. In this particular case, the location was too remote to be practical, and keeping the facilities running would have required a regular flow of money for which there was no budget. So, instead of letting the facilities rot, the municipality let EKPAZ have them. One thing is sure: for EKPAZ, the modern housing constituted a huge improvement over the old jailhouse.

And so on Easter Sunday of 2002 we went to visit the new facilities of EKPAZ. We were greeted by a handful of friendly faces; a couple of them were employees, most were volunteers. They had all gathered there on that day for a certain tradition that is very strong in Greece: the roasting of the lamb, happening each year on Easter Sunday.

This is one of the many paradoxes of the environmental movement in Greece: in any other country of the Western World, a large percentage of those involved with environmentalism, and especially those involved with the protection of animals, would be vegetarian if not vegan. This would have prevented the slightest notion of any kind of roasting of any kind of animal from coming up as a suggestion, but not in Greece, which has a virtually non-existent vegetarian culture. As a result, it is perfectly possible in Greece to see people attending to injured wild animals with determination, devotion, and self-sacrifice, while at the same time, a little bit further away, the exact same people are roasting an animal that had the misfortune of being neither wild, nor injured.

This is not to say that either me or Angelica were vegetarians; we were omnivorous like the rest, but as I like to say, "not fanatic about it". Apparently, we had some slightly different sensitivities. We did not indicate any great interest in standing around the roasting of the lamb, because it is, quite frankly, a ghastly sight to behold. So, it was quickly agreed that one of the volunteers would give us a tour of the facilities.

Being admitted in the place, despite it being closed to the public on that day, and then having a tour guide all for ourselves, made us feel like we were guests of honor. We were very grateful for that.

First we visited the veterinarian's cabin, which was a tiny house consisting of just one room, and maybe a bathroom. It was furnished with an examination table, and benches and shelves with medical supplies and equipment. I do not know much about medical things, but my impression was that it was decently equipped and certainly well kept. I am sure that more equipment would be useful, if only there was enough money to buy it. The lady working there was Maria Ganoti, a well-known figure in environmental circles in Greece. I suppose that people in her line of work do not take days off very often, because the injured animals will not stop arriving just because it is their day off.

Sure enough, we were hardly done with the introductions when I saw through the window a motorcycle arriving outside, and parking in a hurry. It was a BMW R1150GS, as huge and formidable as expensive. The rider, dressed in impeccable (and also quite expensive) motorcycle gear got off the saddle, picked up a carton box from the luggage compartment, and rushed into the clinic.

He was a very tall, and ridiculously handsome young man. His long hair and unshaven look tried, but failed, to make him look rough; you could tell he was a rich kid living the good life. I thought that he might be some kind of celebrity who chooses to invest his free time in activities with a noble cause instead of whatever it is that celebrities otherwise do with their free time.
A re-imagining of the motorcycle and the rider with the help of Google Gemini.

In poor countries like Greece, where disposable income is rare, people tend to have more pressing needs to attend than the protection of the environment or the well-being of animals; thus, the affluent tend to be over-represented within the tiny environmental movement. Heck, come to think of it, even I could be considered as an example of this phenomenon: my comparatively decent salary of a Software Engineer gave me the luxury of not having to worry whether I would be able to pay the rent at the end of each month, and oh, look! what a coincidence, I was also there on a BMW motorcycle—albeit only an F650, which is half the size and less than half the price of an R1150GS—but nonetheless a symbol of Almost Certainly Making Ends Meet™. Quite often we are unaware of the privileges we enjoy.

The motorcycle man extended his arms with great purpose to hand the box to Maria. She took it, and he solemnly lowered his arms as someone whose mission had been accomplished. He stayed to see what was going to happen with the box. We were all very curious to see what was in it.

Maria opened the box, reached inside, and took out one of the most beautiful creatures I have seen in my life. It was a little falcon. His plumage was not particularly fancy, just shades of grey, (so, I suppose he was male,) but around his eyes and at the base of the beak he had those incredibly bright orange pigments that made him look completely out of this world. (Either that, or, I thought, I do not really know much about this world.)

According to research I did for this post more than two decades later, he must have been a Red-footed falcon (falco vespertinus). The Greek name appears to be Μαυροκιρκίνεζο. This photo that I found barely does any justice to what my eyes saw back then: the photo is very, very nice; what I saw was incredible.
Red-footed falcon, photo by Michele Mendi, from lipu.it

Maria held the little falcon in her hands, and with her fingers she carefully felt every millimeter of it. Within a few moments she knew what was wrong with the little fella: he had a broken wing. She started to apply a bandage that would immobilize it and allow it to heal. She did it with such dexterity that it was obvious that she had done the same thing an untold number of times before.

We considered ourselves very lucky and grateful to be given the opportunity to witness that incident and to see Maria at work.

Since I was involved with Greenpeace, an organization which, contrary to popular belief, is not involved in the rescue, rehabilitation, or sheltering of wild animals, I could not help but bring to mind some of the nuances of the situation: Greenpeace does environmental campaigns, political lobbying, legal actions, and nonviolent direct actions with the intention, among other things, of protecting wildlife by preserving their natural habitats, or by bringing an end to human activities such as whaling. However, Greenpeace will not do anything for an individual wild animal in need of help, other than perhaps contacting another organization that specializes in that type of thing. From the perspective of Greenpeace, injured wild animals like that little falcon are but statistics.

Now, do not get me wrong: of course I did deeply care for that particular little falcon, and I was glad that he was being cared for, and I sincerely hoped that he, personally, would make it; but from a global perspective, the rescue of that little falcon was probably not the best use of the resources of the environmental movement as a whole.

I try not to worry about it too much, but it is worth keeping somewhere in the back of the mind that we do not have the resources to transport every injured wild bird by BMW R1150GS.

Wildlife rescue can, in a sense, be thought of as collectively being too busy mopping the floor to turn off the faucet. In fact, we rescue wild animals largely because it makes us feel better, not because it is the most effective thing we could be doing to solve the problem. That is what Greenpeace tries to optimize, and that is why Greenpeace is different; but of course, the human need to be compassionate, the bearing of witness to suffering, and the immense urgency of a life about to be lost unless cared for, cannot be brushed aside. And so here we are, at EKPAZ.

We proceeded to a building where many injured wild birds were kept. There were storks, cranes, flamingos, swans, herons, pelicans, and other kinds of birds that I don't even know their names. They all seemed pretty miserable. Our guide assured us that they were all going to make it, they just had to stay in the facility for a while to recuperate, but they would eventually regain their health and most of them would be released back in the wild.

EKPAZ was performing releases of wild animals about twice a year, and they often organized them as events that people could attend and witness. We had actually attended such an event the year before.
A release event by EKPAZ; from ekpaz.com

We inquired about the causes that resulted in these birds being there, in need of care. She said that in virtually all cases, the cause is humans. She said that a small percentage of the cases are accidents; for example, birds with a large wing span may, on a rare occasion, be shocked by overhead power lines. Those are the cases where humans are only indirectly responsible. However, she said that the vast majority of those birds were there because they had been shot.

And that, despite the fact that all of them belong to species that are never legal to hunt.

This is the sad reality of "sport" hunting in Greece: laws and regulations governing hunt exist like in any other civilized country; shooting those animals is a criminal offense; but the state lacks the resources necessary to enforce the laws, and many, if not most hunters, regard the laws as having a purely decorative function.

The last time a Greek chose to die in order to be in abidance by the law was two and a half thousand years ago.

Keeping such a large number of birds in an enclosed space had a very unfortunate consequence: the room stank with not just the worst stench that I had ever experienced in my life, but I would dare say, a stench that was worse than any stench imaginable. Our guide did not seem to have much of an issue with it; I suppose it is something that you get used to after a while; but while I stood there, I started feeling like I was under physical assault. When we exited the building I was very glad to be able to breathe again.

Then we started walking down a paved path, towards a little house that stood apart from the rest of the buildings.

While on that path, we admired the beautiful view ahead of us: through an opening between two hills on either side we could see some more of the hills of Aegina, then a bit of sea, (part of the Saronic gulf between Aegina and the Peloponnese,) then out in the distance a Peloponnesian mountain range, and then out in the extreme distance yet one more Peloponnesian mountain range. For the needs of this post I managed to find a photo showing that exact same view, albeit under somewhat hazy conditions.
Paved path with a view, leading to small house; photo from ekpaz.com

The path led us in front of the outdoor cages, which were for animals that were in a bit better shape than the ones in the enclosed building.

I think we saw only one animal that was not a bird; it was a wild boar. One might wonder how come the vast majority of animals under the care of EKPAZ are birds. I do not know for sure, but I think the answer has to be something along these lines: we humans have almost wiped out most of the indigenous wildlife in Greece, and continue to murder whatever small populations are left; those populations are so small by now, that injured individuals in need of care are very few and far apart. In contrast, almost all birds are migratory; the north ends of their migration paths tend to be far away north of Greece, and the south ends are far away south, which means that for a large part of the year they live elsewhere, so as much as we would want to, we do not get the chance to exterminate them. On each migration season, however, the land is inundated with large numbers of wildlife available for the slaughter. So, in a few words, the over-representation of birds in EKPAZ probably reflects the fact that almost no other wildlife exists in the country anymore, and the birds exist only because they are passing by.

That having been said, EKPAZ will provide care for any wild animal as long as they have the means for it. Years ago they used to have wolves, up to nine of them at one time. However, in 1992, Arcturos was founded in Northern Greece, an organization specifically for the protection of bears and wolves. So, soon afterward, EKPAZ handed their wolves over to Arcturos.

I was once told that at one point EKPAZ even had an arctic fox. Nobody really knows for sure how an arctic fox was found roaming the streets of suburban Attica, but in all likelihood she had escaped from some unknown, clandestine, illegal operation that raises them for their fur.

EKPAZ has no means of providing care to aquatic animals, but luckily there exist other organizations in Greece that care for those, such as The Sea Turtle Protection Society of Greece, (Archelon,) the Hellenic Society For The Study And Protection Of The Monk Seal (MOm,) and a few others.

Back to our tour of the EKPAZ facilities, I was glad to see that the cages for the large birds were spacious, allowing them some freedom of movement. Especially the one for the vultures was huge. We stopped in front of it to look at the vultures. I had never seen one before.

There are four different types of vulture in Greece; one of them is Threatened world-wide, and all four of them are Threatened within Greece. So, vultures are vanishingly rare in the wild. However, despite their scarcity, there are plenty of them at EKPAZ, constituting a much larger than expected proportion of all birds there.

This is happening because they are disliked by people, so they get shot more often. Many people consider them as unclean, macabre, bad luck, and what not, due to their ugly looks and scavenging nature. So, I suppose that "sport" hunters who would have it at nothing to shoot a stork when bored, would probably go out of their way to shoot a vulture. Of course arbitrary human prejudice reigns supreme over naturalist nonsense like compassionate conservation, respect for all of nature, etc.

I could not help but briefly think of the statistics:

  • Of all birds that are hit by birdshot:
    • Four out of five are killed instantly, only one out of five gets away alive with injuries.
      • Of those that sustain injuries:
        • A tiny fraction like 3% to 5% survives on their own; the vast majority die of their injuries later, unless they are rescued.
          • For a bird to be rescued:
            • It must be found by humans. (The vast majority are never found.)
              • The humans must have nothing to do with hunting.
                • The humans must go out of their way to inquire what one is supposed to do when one finds an injured wild animal, and find out that one is supposed to contact EKPAZ.
                  • The humans must contact EKPAZ, which will give them instructions on how to ship the animal to EKPAZ.
                    • The humans must, in their own free time, do what is necessary to have the animal shipped to EKPAZ;
                      • The animal must be still alive by the time it arrives at EKPAZ.

Those exceedingly few birds that had the incredible luck to reach EKPAZ still alive were the ones that we were looking at in the cages in front of us. So, a fair estimate of the situation is that for each one of the hundreds of birds at EKPAZ, thousands of other birds had died of shotgun injuries, and four times that many more had been shot dead. Almost all of them belonging to species that are never legal to hunt.

What is wrong with humans?

We started walking along the last segment of the path, towards the little house at the end of it.

Already from a distance I noticed something strange: two birds were standing in front of the little house, a couple of meters from each other, motionless, doing nothing in particular. One was brownish, short, and stocky, the other was white, tall, and slender. I found that very odd. I looked hard, to rule out the possibility that they were in cages that I could not see, perhaps cages made of net, but that was not the case. The birds were just standing out there in the open. I could not explain this. I would have expected those birds to either be in cages or to have flown away.

As we drew closer, I could tell that the brown one was a hawk, and the white one was a heron. Each of them looked quite all right; it was not like they were missing plumage or body parts. How could these two birds, belonging to very different species, be simply standing at such close proximity to one another? And why would they even be there in the first place?

For a moment I wondered whether they had come to eat the food intended for the birds in the cages, but I immediately crossed out that theory because Aegina is very far away from their natural habitats: the heron likes rivers, lakes, and sweet-water wetlands, while the hawk roams the woodlands of mainland Greece, not the barren islands of the Aegean sea. So, what on earth were those two birds doing there?

Seeing that they were standing motionless, I seriously considered for a moment that they might be embalmed. Of course it is preposterous to think that EKPAZ would have placed two embalmed birds there, but not as preposterous as suggesting that two such birds would have chosen by themselves to come and stand there. But then I noticed a tiny bit of movement, so the embalmment theory went down, too.

The mystery only thickened as we approached, and the birds did not seem to have any interest in flying or even walking away; however, I noticed that our guide was walking towards the birds without showing any signs of surprise, so I figured that this is normal, and it somehow ends up having a logical explanation, which was bound to be revealed shortly.

For the purposes of this post I found photos of two birds that look exactly like those two at EKPAZ.
A white heron (little egret) (Wikipedia); from Wikimedia Commons.
A hawk (long-legged buzzard) (Wikipedia); from Wikimedia Commons.

We were now standing among the birds, practically towering above them, looking at them just as they were looking at us, with their shiny, vigilant, piercing eyes, those marvels of nature that give them a 360-degree view of their surroundings with a level of detail that we humans could only dream of. Both of them looked healthy and beautiful. I could not believe we were so close to them, with nothing separating us, so that we could touch them if we wanted to, and yet they were just standing there, not minding our presence at all.

Our guide went inside the little house and came out holding a bag of some kind of birdfeed. We heard the distinctive sound of dozens of little pellets hitting metal as she poured some of the birdfeed into a container that was on the ground nearby. Gently, and gracefully, the heron walked over to it, and started eating.

Then she went back inside, and came out again, this time holding a piece of raw meat, about the size of a small schnitzel. She put the meat on top of a rock that must have been there for that purpose, and then she lifted the hawk with her hands, (the hawk, incredibly, not minding at all,) and placed the hawk on the rock, right on top of the meat. For a brief moment the hawk kneaded the meat with his feet, and then started shredding it with his claws and eating it.

Finally, our guide explained. She said that both those birds were in perfectly good health, except for one thing:

They were both blind.

She said that even though there was nothing obviously wrong with them, their optic nerves had been severed by birdshot.

Then she said something that struck me both as an interesting new fact and as something so self-evident that I should have guessed on my own:

A blind bird will not fly.

So, this explained why those two birds were just standing there. They were among the substantial percentage of guests of EKPAZ that were never going to be released. They were staying there for life.

I turned my face towards the lady as to keep my welling eyes hidden behind the sunglasses, but to no avail: gravity dragged the teardrops down my face.

We moved on.

The friendly people of EKPAZ invited us to stay and have lunch with them, but added that we would have to wait some more, because the lamb had taken a lot longer than they had expected to properly roast. So, it was not ready yet, despite it being something like 3 o'clock in the afternoon. They seemed to be rather inexperienced in this, and I entertained the thought that this was perhaps in some sense to their credit: maybe none of them had roasted a lamb before.

Due to a combination of factors having to do with the whole experience of visiting the facilities being a bit overwhelming, plus neither of us particularly caring for the taste of lamb, or for participating in traditions, we thanked them, and told them that we would prefer to return to the town. Both of us were very thankful for having been invited and shown around. I was changed, as a person, by the experience.

Cover image: Heron and Hawk, based on raster image created by Google Gemini from a prompt by michael.gr, then traced using InkScape to convert to svg, and then edited as svg.

item.title: Simon Brown at Miro, Amsterdam
item.description:
I went to see a talk by Simon Brown organized by the Amsterdam Java Users Group (JUG) in the (quite awesome, to be honest) facilities of Miro in Amsterdam. (Facilities tour on YouTube)

Simon has a new book out, The C4 Model, published by O'Reilly. It will be available for purchase in the next few days. Simon said that when O'Reilly contacted him about writing a book he told them that he did not have much material, so it would necessarily be a small book. O'Reilly replied that it's okay, times have changed, people do not actually like big books nowadays, they prefer small books. (I guess this is one more way, in the already long list of ways, in which we are witnessing the demise of humankind.) Anyway, the animal on the cover is a Western Tree Hyrax, and no, Simon did not choose it, O'Reilly always chooses the animal.

Since I do not often travel to Amsterdam, I suffered from a bit of anxiety to be there on time, and as a result I arrived there ridiculously early. So, I had the opportunity to have a chat with the very friendly organizer Geertjan Wielenga, who then introduced me to Simon, so I had the chance to have a chat with him too, one-on-one, for a decent length of time, which is something that I was completely unprepared for.

I admire Simon Brown for caring about the same things that I care about, and for having skill and charisma in talking about those things, but the truth is that we disagree in just about everything. (-:=

Simon believes that software architecture should be strictly descriptive (suggestive), whereas I believe it should be prescriptive (authoritative). I said to him that as things stand today, there is nothing to guarantee to me, the architect, that the programmers and the operations-folk have implemented the system exactly as I designed it. Furthermore, as the system evolves, there is nothing to guarantee that the design still matches the implementation.

Simon agreed that this is a bit of an issue, but went on to speak of existing verification tools that somehow compare systems against their intended designs. I told him that I find this to be way too roundabout and clunky. I brought electronic design as an example of what we should ideally have, where a schematic diagram, being an authoritative design document, can be sent to a manufacturing shop that will turn it into a functioning electronic board with close to zero human intervention.

Simon indicated that he was fully familiar with the paradigm, but went on to say that some people would argue that in software we do not need authoritative architecture because we have the code. I indicated that I am well aware of this proposition, and counter-argued that this is equivalent to saying that the design of a one-million-line-of-source-code software system is the million lines of source code that make up that system, which is as preposterous as saying that the design of the Great Wall of China is a listing of all the bricks that make up the Great Wall of China.

Simon indicated that he saw my point but went on to say that model driven architecture was tried in the early 2000s and it was not a success. He mentioned that the failed attempts invariably involved code generation. I think we both agreed that code generation as a central feature of a software architecture toolset is a bad idea. I told him I believe I have a recipe that will make model driven architecture work, but I do not know what to do with it because it is too much work for a single person like me. He told me that I should try my luck with the academia, they tend to like such things.

There are many other ways in which me and Simon disagree.

For example, Simon does not mind UML at all, whereas I abhor UML, as I have explained in my post On UML.

As another example, Simon believes that code is one of the concerns of software architecture. That's what the fourth "C" stands for in his C4 model. In contrast, I believe that architecture need not, and should not, be concerned with code.

Besides the layer of code, Simon is quite insistent in his C4 model that we need exactly three more layers, with fixed responsibilities: Components, Containers, and Context. In his talk he mentioned that people have objected to him that this is quite unmanageable when we have dozens or even hundreds of components inside a container, and his answer is that in this case, we should visualize the components as little circles instead of boxes, which is essentially saying "well, draw them smaller!". In contrast, I favor the notion of Hierarchical System Composition, which means that any component can in turn be a container, encapsulating other components, to an arbitrary level of nesting. Also, a container can act as context for its constituent components, so we do not need context as a separate layer, either. This fundamentally opposes the C4 model which, in a (noble, but amiss) attempt to bring order and simplicity to our discipline, prescribes exactly four layers; no more, no less.

So, when I wrote that we disagree in just about everything, I did really mean it. (-:= Nonetheless, I like the guy. I do not want to sound like I am dissing him.

Among other take-aways from Simon's talk, A.I. does not seem to (currently?) fare particularly well with:

  • creating C4 designs from source code
  • writing source code from C4 designs.

I postulate that an authoritative software design mechanism would fare much better in these regards, because the results of the conversion would be verifiable in an automated fashion.

Cover photo: Simon Brown at Miro Amsterdam, photo by michael.gr, 2026-07-01.
